1:1: Simon Peter is the name of a man, a disciple of Jesus. See the information about him in Part 1 of the Introduction to 2 Peter.
That these people have received a faith implies that God has given that faith to them.
The word by indicates the means through which they received the faith.
1:2: In this culture, letter writers would offer a good wish for the recipient before introducing the main business of the letter.
God is the one who will give grace and peace to believers.
Peter speaks of grace and peace as if they were objects that could increase in size or number.
Here the pronoun you is plural, since Peter is writing to believers in Jesus as a group. Generally, throughout the letter the pronouns “you” and “your” are plural for this same reason.
This could mean: (1) “because of knowing God and Jesus our Lord” or (2) “through knowing God and Jesus our Lord.”
1:3: Peter is speaking of God’s divine power as if it were a living thing that could give something to people. God is the one who is giving, and he uses his divine power to do so.
The word through here indicates the means by which God has given us all things for life and godliness.
This phrase could refer to: (1) God; (2) Jesus.
Here, through indicates the means by which God called us.
1:4: Here, through indicates the means by which God gave his promises.
Peter speaks of people not suffering from the corruption that wicked desires cause as if they had escaped from that corruption.
Here, the world could mean: (1) the place where we all live, where we are surrounded by sinful people and temptations to sin; (2) the system of values that people share who do not honor God.
Here, by indicates the means by which the world became corrupt. It does not indicate the means by which Peter’s addressees escaped corruption.
1:5: The phrase {for} this same {reason} refers to what Peter has just said in the previous verses.
The phrase applying all diligence indicates the means by which one is to do the action of supplying that follows.
Here, applying all diligence is an idiom that means doing one’s best or making the best effort.
The pronoun your is plural here, since Peter is writing to believers in Jesus as a group. Generally, throughout the letter the pronouns “you” and “your” are plural for this same reason.
1:8: Here, these things refers back to the faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love which Peter mentioned in 1:5–7.
Peter speaks of a person who does not possess these qualities as if he were a field that will not produce a crop.

The words barren and unfruitful mean basically the same thing. In combination with the negatives neither and nor, they are used together to emphasize that this person will not be unproductive but will experience great benefits from knowing Jesus.
1:9: The phrase these things refers back to the faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love, which Peter mentioned in 1:5–7.

In this metaphor, Peter speaks of a person who does not possess these qualities as if the person were blind or nearsighted. He means this in a spiritual sense, that this person cannot see what is spiritually important.
Although the words blind and nearsighted have similar meanings, blind is more extreme than nearsighted, and a person cannot be both at the same time.
τοῦ καθαρισμοῦ τῶν πάλαι αὐτοῦ ἁμαρτιῶν
Peter is speaking of forgiving sin as if sin were something that made people dirty and thus required cleansing from God.
1:10: Peter is using the term brothers as a way to directly address his fellow believers in Jesus.
βεβαίαν ὑμῶν τὴν κλῆσιν καὶ ἐκλογὴν ποιεῖσθαι
The words calling and election share similar meanings and both refer to God choosing believers to belong to him. Peter uses them together to emphasize this idea.
The combination of the words certainly not ever here expresses strong emphatic negation.
Here, stumble could mean: (1) abandoning faith in Christ; (2) committing sin.
1:11: Here, in this way refers back to the way of living that includes the faith, goodness, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, brotherly affection, and love, which Peter mentioned in 1:5–7.
1:12: Here, established is used to refer to one being firmly committed to something.
Here, in has the meaning of “in reference to” or “with regard to.”
Here, present is used as if truth were an object that could be there with Peter’s audience. Here it does not refer to present time.
1:13: ἐφ’ ὅσον εἰμὶ ἐν τούτῳ τῷ σκηνώματι
Peter speaks of his body as if it were a tent that he is wearing and will take off. Being in his body represents being alive.
Peter uses arouse to refer to causing his readers to think about these things.
1:14: ταχινή ἐστιν ἡ ἀπόθεσις τοῦ σκηνώματός μου
Peter speaks of his body as if it were a tent that he is wearing and will take off. Being in his body represents being alive, and taking it off represents dying.
ταχινή ἐστιν ἡ ἀπόθεσις τοῦ σκηνώματός μου
Putting off his tent is a nice way to refer to dying.
Suggested footnote: “Peter may be referring here to what Jesus told him, as recorded in John 21:18–19.”
1:15: Peter uses the word departure as a nice way to speak of his death.
1:16: The words power and coming work together to refer to the same thing; they may be translated as a single phrase.

In this clause Peter refers to the second coming of the Lord Jesus to earth. This future event was foreshadowed by the powerful appearance of Jesus known as the “transfiguration,” which is described in Matthew 17:1–8, Mark 9:1–8, and Luke 9:28–36. Peter was an eyewitness of that event.

This phrase indicates the means by which the apostles had made known to others the second coming of Jesus. The apostles based their teaching about the return of Jesus partly on their eyewitness experience.
1:17: Peter refers to God in terms of his Glory. The glory of God is closely associated with God himself and here substitutes for his name.
Son is an important title for Jesus, the Son of God.
1:18: This is a temporal phrase that can begin with “when.”
1:19: The word translated as very certain could refer to: (1) something that is extremely reliable. In this case, Peter is saying in 1:18–19 that we have two reliable witnesses to Jesus’ glory: God’s own voice speaking on the mountain of transfiguration and the extremely reliable prophetic scriptures; (2) something that is confirmed by something else. In this case, Peter is saying that God’s voice on the mountain confirms, or makes even more trustworthy, the prophetic scripture that we already trusted completely.

Peter uses the phrase prophetic word to refer to the entire Old Testament. It does not refer only to those Old Testament books called “the Prophets,” nor only to the predictive prophecies within the Old Testament.

Here the relative pronoun which refers to the prophetic word mentioned in the previous phrase. Peter instructs the believers to pay close attention to the prophetic message, which is the Old Testament.
ὡς λύχνῳ φαίνοντι ἐν αὐχμηρῷ τόπῳ

Peter compares the prophetic word to a lamp that gives light in the darkness. Just as a lamp gives light in order for someone to see in a dark place, so the prophetic word gives believers guidance for how to live properly in this sin-filled world.
Peter speaks of Christ’s second coming by calling it the new day that comes in the morning.
φωσφόρος ἀνατείλῃ ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις ὑμῶν

Peter speaks of Christ as the morning star, which is a star that indicates daybreak and the end of the night. Christ will rise by bringing light into the hearts of believers, ending all doubt and bringing full understanding of who he is.
Here, hearts is a metonym for people’s minds.
The morning star refers to the planet Venus, which is sometimes visible in the sky just before the sun rises, thus indicating that daybreak is near.
1:20: Peter uses first here to refer to the degree of importance. It does not to refer to order in time.
1:21: ὑπὸ Πνεύματος Ἁγίου φερόμενοι, ἐλάλησαν ἀπὸ Θεοῦ ἄνθρωποι
Peter speaks of the Holy Spirit helping the prophets to write what God wanted them to write as if the Holy Spirit carried them from one place to another.
2:1: Here, the people refers specifically to the Israelites.
Here, heresies refers to opinions that are contrary to the teaching of Christ and the apostles.
Here, destruction could refer to: (1) the eternal damnation of those who teach or accept these heresies; (2) the destruction of the faith of those who teach or accept these heresies.
Peter uses the phrase the master who bought to speak of Jesus as the owner of the people he has saved from damnation by paying the penalty for their sins with his death.
Here, swift could mean: (1) their destruction will come soon; (2) their destruction will be sudden or quick.
2:2: Here Peter uses the word follow to refer to someone imitating the actions of someone else, like someone who walks behind another person in the same direction.
Here, licentious acts refers to immoral sexual actions that demonstrate a lack of self-control.
Peter uses the phrase the way of truth here to refer to the Christian faith or how a Christian person lives his or her life.
Peter speaks of the way of truth as if it were a person who could be slandered or shown disrespect.
Peter assumes that his audience will know that unbelievers will be the ones who slander the Christian faith when they see the sensual lives of the false teachers and their followers.
2:3: Here, in indicates the reason for what the false teachers do.
Here, false words are the means by which the false teachers will exploit their victims.
Peter is using the term words to describe the teachings of the false teachers that were conveyed by using words.
οἷς τὸ κρίμα ἔκπαλαι οὐκ ἀργεῖ
Here, for whom indicates that the condemnation is directed again the false teachers.
These two long phrases mean basically the same thing and emphasize that the false teachers will certainly be condemned.
Peter speaks of condemnation and destruction as if they are people who can be idle or sleep.
2:4: This phrase could refer to: (1) chains in a very dark place; (2) a very deep darkness that imprisons them like chains.

The word Tartarus is a term from Ancient Greek religion that refers to the place where evil spirits and wicked men who have died are punished. Some Ancient Jewish literature written in Greek uses Tartarus as a term for the place where God punishes the wicked.
God is the one who handed over the angels who had sinned.
Here, Peter speaks of God imprisoning the angels who sinned like someone who has handed over a criminal to the prison guards for imprisonment.
This phrase refers to the sinful angels mentioned earlier in the verse.
2:5: Here, world refers to the people who lived in it.
As in 2:4, the word spare here means “to refrain from punishing.”
Here, eighth is an idiom used to refer to a group of eight people. It means that Noah was one of only eight people in the ancient world whom God did not destroy.
2:6: This phrase indicates the means by which God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.
2:7: τῆς τῶν ἀθέσμων ἐν ἀσελγείᾳ ἀναστροφῆς
Here, in indicates the content of what the lawless people were doing.
Here, the lawless ones refers to the people who lived in the city of Sodom, where Lot lived.
2:8: Peter uses for here to provide background information about Lot’s life in Sodom. This is to help readers understand why Peter called Lot a righteous person in the previous verse. Peter is not using for here to indicate result.
This clause indicates the time when Lot dwelled in Sodom.
Here, soul refers to Lot’s thoughts and emotions. The immoral behavior of the citizens of Sodom and Gomorrah disturbed him emotionally.
This phrase could mean: (1) the lawless works were the means by which Lot tormented his soul; (2) the lawless works were the reason why Lot tormented his soul.
2:9: Here, in could refer to: (1) when the unrighteous ones will be punished; (2) the point in time up to which the unrighteous ones will be punished.
2:10: Connecting Statement: Peter uses the phrase going after to refer to habitually doing something. This expression is frequently used in the Bible to describe people worshiping false gods or engaging in sexual immorality.
Here, flesh is used to refer to person’s sinful nature.
Here, in indicates that this phrase shows the means by which the wicked people go after the flesh.

Here, authority could refer to: (1) God’s authority, as suggested from the examples of rebelling against God in the previous verses; (2) angelic authority, as suggested by the insulting of “glorious ones” mentioned in the remainder of the verse.
Audacious ones marks the beginning of the second section of this chapter, which continues until the end of 2:22. In this section Peter describes the wicked character and deeds of the false teachers.
Self-willed means “doing whatever one wants to do.”
This clause indicates the time when the false teachers do not tremble.
Here, glorious ones could refer to: (1) spiritual beings, such as angels, demons, or both; (2) important human beings, such as church leaders.
2:11: The words strength and power mean similar things. Peter is using them together for emphasis. Together, the words describe extreme power.
2:12: Peter describes the false teachers by comparing them to unreasoning animals. Just as animals cannot think rationally, neither can these people.
γεγεννημένα φυσικὰ εἰς ἅλωσιν καὶ φθοράν
Here, by nature means that the unreasoning animals (and false teachers by comparison) were destined for capture and destruction due to their very nature as animals born for this purpose.
This clause could refer to: (1) more information about the false teachers; (2) the reason the false teachers will be destroyed.
Here, those things could refer to: (1) the “glorious ones” of 2:10; (2) the Christian teachings that these false teachers are rejecting.
Here, also is used for emphasis and may be translated as “indeed” or “surely.”
This clause indicates the time when the false teachers will be destroyed.
2:13: Peter speaks of the punishment that the false teachers will receive as if it were a wage they had earned.
This phrase indicates the time when the false teachers were reveling.
Peter speaks of the false teachers as if they were stains or blemishes on a garment that cause shame for those who wear it.
The words stains and blemishes share similar meanings. Peter is using them together for emphasis.
2:14: Here, eyes refers to a person’s desires, and eyes full means that a person constantly desires one thing.

This clause could mean: (1) the false teachers constantly desired to have immoral sexual relations with any woman they saw, thereby viewing every women as a potential adulteress; (2) the false teachers were constantly looking for immoral women with whom to have immoral sexual relations.
This clause refers to the actions of the false teachers Peter introduced in 2:1.
This clause refers to the actions of the false teachers Peter introduced in 2:1.
Peter is using hearts to refer to whole persons, including their thoughts, desires, and emotions. The term can thus be translated here with the reflexive pronoun “themselves.”

Peter is using a Hebrew idiom in which a person is said to be a “child” of the thing that characterizes that person. Here, children of cursing refers to people who are cursed by God. He is not speaking of people who curse others.
2:15: Peter uses the metaphor Abandoning the straight way to give an image of walkers leaving a certain pathway. He speaks of the false teachers refusing to live their lives in obedience to the Lord as if they had stopped walking on the Lord’s path.

Here, the straight way refers to the way of living life that is right and pleasing to the Lord. Peter may also be using it here to refer specifically to the Christian faith, similar to his use of “the way of truth” in 2:2.
Here, Peter continues the path metaphor from the previous clause. He describes the wicked lifestyles of the false teachers as if they had been led astray from the straight path.

In this verse, Peter compares the false teachers to Balaam. Peter assumes that his readers will know that he is referring to a story recorded in the Old Testament book of Numbers. In that story, Balaam was hired by wicked kings to curse the Israelites. When God did not allow Balaam to do so, he used wicked women to seduce the Israelites into sexual immorality and idol worship so that God would punish them for their disobedience. Balaam did these wicked things because he wanted to be paid by the wicked kings, but he was eventually killed by the Israelites when they conquered the land of Canaan.
ἐξακολουθήσαντες τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ τοῦ Βοσὸρ
Here, Peter uses the word followed to refer to someone imitating the actions of someone else, like someone who walks behind another person in the same direction.
τῇ ὁδῷ τοῦ Βαλαὰμ τοῦ Βοσὸρ
Here, Peter uses the way of Balaam to refer to how Balaam lived his life.
2:16: This clause could mean: (1) the donkey rebuked Balaam; (2) God rebuked Balaam through the donkey.
This transgression specifically refers to Balaam’s use of wicked women to lead the Israelites into sexual immorality and idolatry.
2:17: Peter speaks of the false teachers to describe their uselessness. People expect springs to provide water to quench thirst, but waterless springs leave thirsty people disappointed. In the same way, false teachers, although they promise many things, are unable to do what they promise.

Peter gives a second figurative description of the uselessness of the false teachers. When people see storm clouds, they expect rain to fall. When the winds from the storm blow the clouds away before the rain can fall, the people are disappointed. In the same way, false teachers, although they promise many things, are unable to do what they promise.
These two metaphors mean similar things. Peter is using them together for emphasis.
This could mean: (1) the gloom is characterized by darkness; (2) the gloom is identical to the darkness.
Here, Peter uses gloom and darkness to refer to hell.
2:18: This clause indicates the means by which the false teachers entice others to sin.
Here, flesh is used to refer to a person’s sinful nature.
Here, licentious acts refers to immoral sexual actions that demonstrate a lack of self-control.
τοὺς ὀλίγως ἀποφεύγοντας τοὺς ἐν πλάνῃ ἀναστρεφομένους

Here, Peter speaks of people who recently became believers as those barely escaping from sinful humanity. He also refers to unbelievers who still live according to their sinful desires as those living in error.
2:19: This clause refers to another means by which the false teachers enticed their followers, continuing from the previous verse.
Here, freedom is a metaphor for the ability to live exactly as one wants.
Peter uses the word themselves here to emphasize the irony of spiritually enslaved people promising spiritual freedom to others.
Peter speaks of people who live sinfully as if they were slaves to sin who need to escape from their captivity.
ᾧ γάρ τις ἥττηται, τούτῳ δεδούλωται
Peter speaks of a person as being enslaved when anything has control over that person, he speaks of that thing as the master of that person.
2:20: Here, For could refer to: (1) another explanation of Peter’s statement “themselves being slaves of destruction” in the previous verse, (2) a transition from what Peter said in the previous verse to what he is going to say in this verse. Here, For does not indicate the reason or result of what was said in the previous verse.
εἰ … ἀποφυγόντες τὰ μιάσματα τοῦ κόσμου
Using a similar metaphor to that in 2:18, here Peter speaks of believers as if they had been slaves to the defilements of the world and have escaped that captivity.
Here, the world refers to human society, which has been corrupted by sin.
Here, Peter speaks of people who seem to have been believers but have returned to living sinfully as if they have become entangled in a net.
2:21: Peter speaks of life as a way or path. This phrase refers to the way of living life that is right and pleasing to the Lord. Peter may also be using it here to refer specifically to the Christian faith, similar to his use of “the way of truth” in 2:2 and “the straight way” in 2:15.
This clause indicates that the next clause describes an event that happened after the event of this clause.
Here, to turn away from is a metaphor that means to stop doing something.
2:22: Peter uses two proverbs to illustrate what the false teachers have done. These proverbs make a figurative comparison: Just as a dog returns to eat its own vomit and a washed pig rolls in the mud again, so these false teachers, who once stopped living a sinful life, have now gone back to living sinfully. Although they knew “the way of righteousness,” they went back to doing the things that defile them morally and spiritually.
A dog is an animal that is considered to be unclean and disgusting by Jews and many cultures of the Ancient Near East. Therefore, calling someone a dog was an insult.
A pig is an animal that is considered to be unclean and disgusting by Jews and many cultures of the Ancient Near East. Therefore, calling someone a pig was an insult.
3:1: Beloved ones refers here to those to whom Peter is writing, which can be extended to all believers.
διεγείρω ὑμῶν ἐν ὑπομνήσει τὴν εἰλικρινῆ διάνοιαν
Here, Peter uses arouse, as if the minds of his readers are asleep, to refer to causing his readers to think about these things.

Although the word pure usually refers to something being uncontaminated or not mixed with something else, Peter uses it here to indicate that his readers have minds which have not been deceived by the false teachers.
3:2: Peter is using words here to describe the prophecies of the Old Testament prophets that were conveyed by using words, especially those prophecies about the future return of Christ.
Here, prophets refers to the Old Testament prophets whom Peter also referred to in 1:19–21.
This phrase indicates the means by which the command of the Lord and Savior was given to Peter’s readers.
Here, your apostles could refer to: (1) the apostles who proclaimed the teachings of Christ to Peter’s readers or ministered to them in some way; (2) all apostles, who belong to all Christians.
3:3: Peter uses first here to refer to the degree of importance. It does not to refer to order in time.
κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι
Here, Peter uses going to refer to habitually doing something, like someone who walks toward something.
κατὰ τὰς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας αὐτῶν πορευόμενοι
Here, lusts refers to sinful desires that are opposed to God’s will.
3:4: ποῦ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ
The mockers ask this rhetorical question to emphasize that they do not believe that Jesus will return.
ποῦ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ
Here, Where is used to ask what has happened to the promise. The mockers are not asking for the location of something.
ποῦ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπαγγελία τῆς παρουσίας αὐτοῦ
Here, promise refers to the fulfillment of the promise that Jesus will return.
Here, his coming refers to the return of the Lord Jesus to earth.
ἀφ’ ἧς γὰρ οἱ πατέρες ἐκοιμήθησαν

Here, the fathers is used. It could refer to: (1) the Old Testament ancestors of the Israelites, often called “the patriarchs.”; (2) those leaders of the first generation of Christians who had died by the time Peter wrote this letter.
Here, fell asleep is a euphemism meaning they died.
πάντα οὕτως διαμένει ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς κτίσεως
Here, all things is an exaggeration the mockers use to argue that nothing in the world has ever changed, so it cannot be true that Jesus will return.
3:5: ἐξ ὕδατος καὶ δι’ ὕδατος συνεστῶσα
This clause refers to God causing the land to come up out of and through the water, gathering the bodies of water together to make the land appear.
Here, the word of God refers to the God’s specific commands by which the earth was created.
3:6: Here, at that time refers to the time when the world existed before the flood. It does not refer to the exact time when the universe was created.
This phrase indicates the means by which the ancient world was destroyed.
3:7: Here, word refers to “the word of God,” which Peter said in 3:5–6 was the means by which the heavens and earth were created and a flood destroyed the world.
Here, Peter uses fire to refer to what fire does, which is burn.
Here, for could refer to: (1) the purpose for which God is keeping the present heavens and earth; (2) the point in time up to which God is keeping the present heavens and earth.
3:8: ὅτι μία ἡμέρα παρὰ Κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη
Here, with the Lord means “in the judgment of the Lord.”

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize that God does not perceive of time the same way that humans do. What might seem to be a short or long time for people would not seem so for God.
3:9: Here, promise refers to the fulfillment of the promise that Jesus will return.
Here, some refers to the “mockers” introduced in 3:3 and anyone else who believed that the Lord is slow to fulfill his promises, because Jesus had not yet returned.
3:10: Peter speaks of the day when God will judge everyone as if it were a thief who will come unexpectedly and take people by surprise.
Here, elements could refer to: (1) the basic elements that make up the natural universe; (2) the heavenly bodies, such as the sun, moon, and stars.
Here, being burned up refers to the means by which the elements will be destroyed.
γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα εὑρεθήσεται
Here, deeds refers to the actions of people on the earth.
γῆ καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῇ ἔργα εὑρεθήσεται
Here, found indicates that the removal of the heavens and elements will leave the earth and what has been done on it exposed for God to see and judge.
3:11: Peter is using the question form for emphasis.
3:12: Here, waiting for and hastening are two things Peter wanted his readers to do while also living holy and godly lives, as stated in the previous verse.
This phrase indicates the means by which the heavens will be destroyed.
Here, elements could refer to: (1) the basic elements that make up the natural universe; (2) the heavenly bodies, such as the sun, moon, and stars.
This phrase indicates the means by which the heavens will be destroyed.
3:13: Here, promise could refer to: (1) God’s promise to create a new heavens and earth, as promised in Isaiah 65:17 and Isaiah 66:22; (2) the promise of Jesus’ second coming, as in 3:4.
Here, righteousness is spoken of as though it were a person who could dwell somewhere.
3:14: Here, beloved ones refers to those whom Peter is writing to, which can be extended to all believers.
The words spotless and blameless share similar meanings. Peter is using them together for emphasis.
Here, in peace could refer to: (1) having peace with God.
3:15: τὴν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν μακροθυμίαν, σωτηρίαν ἡγεῖσθε
Because the Lord is patient, the day of judgment has not yet happened. This gives people an opportunity to repent and be saved, as Peter explained in 3:9.
Peter is using the term brother to refer to Paul as a fellow believer in Jesus.
3:16: Here, the context suggests that Paul is the author of the letters.
ἃ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς καὶ ἀστήρικτοι στρεβλοῦσιν
Here, distort is used to describe changing the meaning of a statement in order to give a false meaning like twisting something so that it changes shape.
Here, the other scriptures refers to both the entire Old Testament and the New Testament texts that had been written by the time Peter wrote this letter.
3:17: Here, beloved ones refers to those whom Peter is writing to, which can be extended to all believers.
ἵνα μὴ … ἐκπέσητε τοῦ ἰδίου στηριγμοῦ
Here, Peter speaks of steadfastness as if it were a possession that believers could lose.
Here, Peter uses led astray to describe people being deceived into living wickedly by false teachers as if they had been led away from the straight path.
This phrase indicates the means by which one might be led astray.
3:18: Here, grow is used to express experiencing or having something in increasing amounts.
